utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have kept you waiting. It was my fault. I was discussing various things. Who's going to begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Court's permission, I will. We have several issues that we'd like to discuss today and get some rulings on, if we can. The first is related to the issue of dead witnesses, and specifically the statements of Midhat Haskic and Erik Friis-Pedersen that the Prosecution wishes to have admitted into evidence. Secondly, is the issue of the site visit that the Prosecution has proposed. The third concerns a request previously made by the Trial Chamber to the Blaskic Trial Chamber relating to the closed testimony of three witnesses. The fourth relates to the protective order that has been entered into; this case needs a slight modification in order to make it reciprocal. We have an ex parte matter of a very short duration that we need to take up with the Trial Chamber. There is an issue related to the secret witnesses that have been called by the Prosecution and subsequent recantations of the need for protective measures. Then we have several issues related to the conduct of expeditious and fair trial. There are five issues that I've been able to identify. They are as follows: the issue of the two weeks' advance notice of the order of witnesses that has been ordered by the Trial Chamber; the use of leading questions; the matter of exhibits, and fair advance notice of what those exhibits are going to be, so that we don't have to scramble through them in the Trial Chamber; the issue of notes and diaries prepared by witnesses; and then an issue relating to certain standing objections in order to eliminate the necessity for objections and interruption of witnesses' testimony. With the Court's permission, I will address the issue of dead witnesses and Ms. Ers Haskic and Friis-Pedersen; the Blaskic issue; I'll take up the ex parte matter; and I will handle the two weeks' advance notice and leading-questions issues. Mr. Stein will take up the site visit issue, the protective order issue, the matter relating to secret witnesses, and the fair trial matters related to exhibits, notes, and diaries, and standing objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we'll do is this. We'll take these items one by one. Perhaps the Registrar could do something about the building works, please. Thank you. The sensible course, I think, would be to deal with some of these matters. Necessarily, it will have to be dealt with in private session, I think. But on the issue of dead witnesses, to begin with the first, this is a matter which we have discussed. It has been outstanding for some time. As I observed on the last occasion, it's certainly not usually a matter for the Defence to determine when the application should be made, since it is the Prosecution's application to have the evidence admitted, not, as it were, your application. Now, Mr. Sayers, what is it you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Obviously, Mr. President, if the Court feels that this is not the appropriate time and if the Prosecution feels that this is not the appropriate time to address those issues, then so be it. But I personally cannot imagine that there is anything more to be argued concerning these issues. I think that full submissions have been made to the Court; they simply can be highlighted in oral argument. As I understand it, with respect to Mr. Haskic, anyway, there are some issues relating to the death certificate that need to be addressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Mr. Nice said yesterday that there was some evidence which he was going to call which would bear upon that issue and, if that is right, it would be presumably more sensible to hear that and rule in the light of it. Mr. Nice, perhaps you can help. Is that the position, as I understood it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. In each case -- that is, Friis-Pedersen and Haskic -- there is more evidence yet to come before the Trial Chamber on the topics to which each of those deceased witnesses' statements could bear. And it seems to me, rather than address argument against the backdrop of projected evidence, it would be more helpful for the Chamber and make more sense to have all the evidence in, and then for the argument about the dead witness to be addressed in light of that evidence. It will then be possible to know to what extent the evidence is freestanding and to what extent it is confirming earlier evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that could affect our ruling in terms of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- how necessary the evidence is. Mr. Sayers, it seems sensible to deal with it when we know the full context in which the evidence is going to be sought to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: May I make just one point in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I fully agree with the Prosecution, if there is confirmatory evidence regarding the actual facts in dispute regarding Mr. Haskic, for example, actual corroborative evidence of the facts about which he testifies, not about prior meetings or prior issues, then I'm in full agreement; it may be best to defer that. But with respect to Mr. Friis-Pedersen, it strikes me that that's a completely discrete argument. The argument is this. It's very simple. Mr. Friis-Pedersen's testimony, his sworn testimony in the Blaskic case, has already been admitted in this case under the rule of Aleksovski. So what we have now is an effort on the part of the Prosecution to have his statement admitted as well, and we think that, for the reasons stated in the Tulica dossier decision, amongst other things, there's absolutely no reason not to do that. This man was cross-examined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we hear the argument. I think it would be more convenient to deal with any dead witnesses together, no matter what the arguments are. The next point you raised, to do with a visit. It may be more appropriate to deal with that in a closed session in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we leave that for the moment. The next matter was the Blaskic order and the closed testimony. Would you remind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't believe that there is any need to go into closed session about that because I don't need to mention the names. I think the Court will have in mind that on August the 6th a request was issued to the Blaskic Trial Chamber to have the closed session testimony of three witnesses released to the parties in this case. And no action has been taken on that, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let me draw that attention to the senior legal officer, and the matter will be pursued. Perhaps, if again there is no response within 28 days, you can raise the matter again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will ask for a response, please. Yes. There's an issue on protective orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Stein will address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, is it a matter which we could deal with in open session or is it a matter for closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It matters not either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Deal with it now then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. We would essentially ask that the Court amend the protective order to make it reciprocal. In particular, I would give you up a draft of the section of the protective order that we would like to have changed, if I may. A copy for the Prosecution and the Registrar so we won't be dealing in the abstract. May it please the Court. Pursuant to Rule 73(a) and 75(a) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and paragraph 11 of this Court's 15 January 1999 order for measures to protect victims and witnesses, we essentially move to amend certain parts of the protective order relative to the announcement of and contact with defence witnesses. We will presumably be obliged shortly, and I use the term advisedly, to produce a list of defence witnesses. The Prosecution, of course, has insisted on a protective order relative to the witnesses they have named in their submissions. We, with great care, have studied that order and we realise it is not reciprocal. The sad part about what has happened in the former Yugoslavia is there is a perception by witnesses who I have interviewed, by witnesses that other members of our team have interviewed, of concern, whether it's legitimate concern or not is not the point, about being contacted by either members of the Prosecution themselves or investigators. And so we essentially ask for the same kinds of protections with regard to defence witnesses that are already extant with regard to Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So this is an order which will apply when the defence begins?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Exactly. Or 30 days before because we'll be announcing our witnesses by then. I think the specifics of the order are set out very clearly, the proposed order, in the draft I've handed up. The Prosecution will suffer no prejudice by it. We have suffered no prejudice by living under the order for as long as we have, and it would be advisable to enter into such an order. Certainly the Rules contemplate that the orders entered for protection of witnesses be reciprocal. Rule 75(a) authorises the Trial Chamber to adopt measures for the protection of witnesses "at the request of either party." This issue was forecast in Pre-Trial proceedings, in pleadings regarding the protective order. Certainly the Prosecution was aware of it as early as 23 October 1998, and in our pleadings in the fall of 1998, and we think now is an appropriate time to deal with and have the Court resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution have any observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't seen this draft before, therefore, I haven't been able to integrate it with the original order. Protective orders is something that's been dealt with principally by Mr. Scott, and I didn't know this was going to be raised this morning. There is no immediate pressure on having this agreed. Maybe have until next week just to look at it, and if there is no objection, we'll let you know straightaway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stein, wouldn't it be simpler, from a formal point of view, because what you are suggesting is a review of a previous order for protective measures, and therefore we have to have the previous order in order to make comparisons with what Mr. Nice had just said. But would it be simpler, since it's going to apply only, as you said, once the Defence has begun to present its case or a little time before, you spoke about a month, wouldn't it be better for you to have another plan, another draft or, rather, another order rather than -- rather than one that would be changing this one? Wouldn't that be easier? Because it's a formal issue. I think it would be easier for you to make a request in proper form, with a proposal for an order for protective measures that we could study, and at that point we would have the response from the Prosecutor and we would take our decision in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We can certainly proceed that way -- it is on. We can certainly proceed in that way. In this age of word processing, the reason that I attached what I did and gave it to you, for those of us who are semi-computer literate or not, is you can see on the draft the old part of the order that we want to strike and the new part that we want to enter. But we certainly can file a formal pleading setting out the change in the order, if it makes it easier, and we'll be glad to do that. It won't take but a few minutes. But I chose this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution needs some time to look at it. Obviously, we need a bit of time, because it may be helpful. There is no need to enter a formal pleading with the argument and all of that sort of thing, but to enter the proposed order which you wish to suggest to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'll clean that up and have that within 48 hours or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be the best way to proceed. The next matter is described as secret witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. What we'd like to have at this time is a review of the process relative to secret witnesses. We believe thus far two at least of the secret witnesses have revealed the process which creates a problem. Two of the witnesses, I'm sure Your Honours are aware because they are not public, Mr. Cicak and Mr. Kljuic, we were told were secret witnesses. The Prosecution flooded the Chamber with many prejudicial statements why they wanted to be secret witnesses. When they came actually to The Hague, they said, "We don't want to be a secret witness. We want our testimony for the world." In the meantime, we had been prejudiced because, A, only four of our team could work on the matter; B, the discovery attendant to the witness's testimony was delayed until ten days before their appearance; and last, but not least, what is not particularly apparent is that the process by which we have to set up our affairs and our own shop to make sure that no one has access to these particular witnesses statements is difficult. Moreover, some of the witnesses bring huge amounts of documents and things with them. So in ten days we are asked to analyse a large amount of material. What we ask the Court, not to eliminate the process of secret witnesses. That would be inappropriate. But before the Prosecution is allowed to use and embark on the secret witness process, that the witness sign an affirmation presented to the Court as to why he wants secret witness status and that he does in fact want said status. That would eliminate the entire problem. That's all I have to say on that particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, even after he signs that affirmation, he might still change his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. Absolutely true. But at least we'll have a reason in advance to know of his status. And if he changes his mind, that might be -- in fact, become a credibility issue. But there are exigencies, of course, that we have to expect. I guess what I am really saying is there appears to be, and I can't say this with certainty, a gap between the Prosecutor's office and the witness or whoever contacts the witnesses from the Prosecutor's office on the secret witness status. We are trying to close that gap. If someone from the Prosecution's office believes the witness wants secret witness status, have the witness himself sign an affirmation in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly hope there is not a gap between the office and the witness. There is, of course, sometimes a difference between the attitude of the witness ahead of getting here and ahead of overcoming the practical difficulties of getting here without being interrupted and disturbed, and the way he feels when he is here. Of course, when they are here, they are all subject to the emphasis that I personally place on witnesses giving evidence in public whenever possible. And that may account in part or whole for apparent changes of mind. I would resist the suggestion that there has to be some routine whereby witnesses sign an affirmation setting out their requested measure of protection. That would create all sorts of practical difficulties, I think, and would not relieve the Tribunal of making a decision on a case-by-case basis. I would ask the existing routine to stay in place, that is to say, that the Tribunal will consider applications on a case-by-case basis. Obviously, if it has questions or concerns, when material is presented in written form, it can seek further clarification from us. If it wants something particular from a particular witness, it can do so. But it can be confident that so far as I am concerned, and I hope all of my team, the clear emphasis with all witnesses is on giving evidence in public, and if that has occasionally led to an apparent change of position, I'm sorry. But I think it's a change in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me, if I can for the Court, merely remind the Court that Mr. Kljuic, for instance, came to Court and said, "I never wanted to be a secret witness. I have to tell the world about what went on." Now, there must have been some miscommunication between the Prosecutor's office and Mr. Kljuic, because he was the subject of a secret witness application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or Mr. Kljuic changed his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Either or. But this proposal would elucidate that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, when you work with a witness, your investigators see the witness, they gather the substantial information, and the witness says that he intends to testify under that circumstance. Do you have him sign his statement as to the substance? Would it be difficult for you also to have him sign a declaration about the way and the manner that he wishes to testify? Would that disturb you so much? I am speaking about the future witnesses. For those who have already been here it's a closed issue. But when you make a statement, perhaps they could also sign as to the substance and as to the form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think there will be a problem when witnesses are seen at the time that the decision is made for them to come and give evidence. But there are witnesses, I think, with whom we have no direct contact ahead of their coming to the Tribunal and with whom negotiations are made sometimes via third parties, of necessity, and sometimes via other agencies. And so in those cases, of course we wouldn't be able to have a statement contemporaneous with their first expression of intention and willingness to attend. But where we do see a witness directly, yes, I don't see any problem with that, and I can endeavour to ensure that that is all done for all future such witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or in the case of the other witnesses, you simply send an affirmation or declaration or something of that sort through to them and ask them to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If only it should be that easy. I can deal with it ex parte, but there are one or two cases where I'm afraid that simply wouldn't be possible. But I think there are only one or two cases outstanding, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask you that, as to the size of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very small. It's a very small, outstanding problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will consider this matter. The principle, of course, is that evidence is given in public session and we would encourage anything to that end. We recognise that in some cases there will be good reason why this can't be done. But we also recognise that it does place burdens on the defence, if such a procedure is followed, as has been outlined. What we shall order is this: That normally the witness should sign a declaration that he wishes the matter to be heard in the way which is suggested, i.e., secretly; that if there are reasons why that can't be done, that will have to be explained to the Court. The statement should also set out briefly why the witness is requesting that the matter be dealt with in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next issues are, I think, if I have it right, under the heading of expeditious trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We've grouped these issues together, and I don't think they will take particularly long to address. They are all under the heading of fair and expeditious trial issues. At the beginning of the discussion, I certainly want to stress -- and I hope that the Court is under the impression that this has been the case -- that the Defence has been bending over backwards to try to accommodate the expediency with which evidence is brought in. It's embarrassing and unprofessional for us to have to scramble around at the last minute to try to come up with a comprehensive, short, cross-examination plan. That takes unnecessary time, goes into unnecessary subjects, and it's extraordinarily difficult, once you have come up with a plan in advance without knowing exactly what subjects the witness is going to testify about, to eliminate, on the spur of the moment, areas of questioning which, had you had a little bit more advance notice or time to prepare, a little more time for reflection, you wouldn't have to go into. And that would save the Trial Chamber's time and patience. The first two issues that I want to bring up are related directly to those matters. The first is -- actually, both of these issues involve a large number of witnesses identified by the Prosecution as witnesses it intends to call, and therefore for whom the Defence has to prepare; 375, I think, is the number. I don't think anyone really believes that that will ultimately be the number, but we don't have any definitive number yet, and that's a problem for the Court, but especially for the people that have to prepare for the cross-examination of these witnesses. And so the two issues that I would like to raise initially are the use of leading questions. First, the Prosecutor itself sought a prohibition, as no doubt the Trial Chamber will remember, on the use of leading questions on direct examination. I think that as procedures have evolved in this case, there's been a move away from that, and perhaps it's a legitimate and a good move under the appropriate circumstances. And those circumstances are, I think, when we are given an accurate -- and I stress, an accurate -- forecast of what the witness is supposed to be saying sufficiently in advance to be able to identify -- 24 hours would be sufficient, as has been occasionally the practice with respect to past witnesses; 24 hours would be sufficient to specify to the Trial Chamber the matters upon which we do not object to having the Prosecution lead its own witnesses through the evidence. But I do stress that we do object to the use of leading questions when we're given these offers of proof 24 seconds before the witness testifies, as was the case yesterday, especially in regard to witnesses that the Prosecution orally characterises as important witnesses, and especially when there's such a substantial deviation between the forecast of what they're supposedly going to say and what they actually do say. So we would urge the Trial Chamber to hold the Prosecution to what it had originally sought, when these offers of proof are not provided more than 24 hours in advance, and that is, do not lead your own witness through the testimony. We think it's unfair. It's unfairly surprising, and it puts unfair burdens upon the Defence to have to make snap decisions, once again on the spur of the moment, as to areas which are appropriate subjects of leading or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt, Mr. Sayers, to say this. The first thing that you are asking for, although you haven't in terms, is a definitive list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, as I recollect, we have ordered a Status Conference towards the end of this month, the 26th of November --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- to my recollection. And the Prosecutor is going to provide us with a list. As for the other matters, this is -- the whole question of leading questions is partly a matter of practice, and where I come from, you can't lead on matters which are in dispute. That's the essential rule, and the reason is that if you do, it makes the evidence worthless, because it's counsel giving the evidence. But that said, on matters which aren't in dispute, matters of bringing the witness to the point of proof, to the real matters which are in dispute, then leading questions play an important role; it gets the witness there as quickly as possible. We have been through this question of the offers of proof and heard the Prosecution on the subject, and their answer always is, "Well, we do the best we can, but we have a limited amount of time because of the witnesses arriving fairly late in The Hague and us having to get the witnesses ready." We've encouraged the use of these offers of proof as a way of concentrating the evidence in a particular area, and we would not wish to discourage their use. There is no burden on the Defence in relation -- or should be no burden on the Defence -- in relation to saying what is disputed and what isn't. No one would expect you, on getting a document, immediately to be able to respond to it. I think it's the ideal situation if you have it 24 hours in advance so that you can, and I would hope that the Prosecution have that in mind and try and comply as much as possible. But I guess, in some cases, their answer is that it's physically impossible to do it before then, in which case there is no burden on you to say what they can lead on and what they can't. But I think some intelligent, as it were, use of leading questions is perfectly permissible. And I think to this extent there's a burden on the Defence, to say, objecting, "Don't lead from now on."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If leading is going on, "Don't lead on this point." And it's an important part, if I may say so, because it does indicate what's in dispute and warns the Prosecution, and what isn't. If that's of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Of course it's of assistance, Mr. President, in the abstract, but as a practical matter, when you're confronted with something that's 25 pages long and maybe 165 paragraphs -- I mean, I'm not telling the Court anything that it doesn't already know -- it's extraordinarily difficult for us to read that and assimilate it in any reasonable period of time, and then react to it instantly, without constantly standing up and interrupting and -- I hope I can say -- incurring the risk of the Court's wrath by appearing to be obstructive when we don't mean to be, and we simply mean to say that these matters are in dispute. And oftentimes the pace of leading questions is so fast that sometimes you're through a subject before you have the opportunity to say, "Objection."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, speaking for myself, I do not object when counsel, even from a sitting position, shouts out, "Don't lead," and that is the way to stop it. If there is a torrent of leading questions, as it were, on a matter which is in dispute, then of course the Prosecution should be stopped. And it's in fact helpful if the Defence do say, "Don't lead," because then the Court knows that these are matters on which there should not be leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That is helpful, Mr. President. I hope that it won't be necessary, but in the event that we get deliveries at the last second, so to speak, then we will try our best to inform the Prosecution that it should not lead as to particular paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And if you have a situation with the document arriving just before the witness gives evidence, then by all means say so, so that the Court knows what the position is. And if you do make your objections in that form, then it will be understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. The second point that I wanted to address in this regard is related somewhat, and it's somewhat different from the point that you raised regarding the universe of witnesses. It's really an issue that's related to the scheduling order that was entered on March the 22nd. We did not want necessarily to bring this to the Trial Chamber's attention. We've had a torrent of correspondence with the Prosecution, but I think, frankly, the time has come when we need to insist upon exactly what the Court ordered. And the Court ordered two very simple things. In paragraph 5 of the scheduling order that was entered on March the 22nd, the Court required that "The Prosecution shall provide the Trial Chamber and the Defence with not less than two weeks' notice of the witnesses to be called"; and then the second thing was, "and shall draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the relative importance of certain witnesses as listed." Now, as far as I'm aware, there have been about three occasions upon which we have received this two weeks' advance notice in the seven months of trial. There have been 54 witnesses called so far. Many of the witnesses who were indicated in the three two-week notices that we've got are actually witnesses who have, A, not been called, or not called in that order. So once again it's a matter of preparation, a matter of expediency, trying to accelerate the fairness of the process and streamlining our cross-examination. I think we're entitled to exactly what the Court ordered, except in extraordinary circumstances, obviously, which can perhaps be addressed on a case-by-case basis. But it seems to me, Your Honour, if I may say so, that given the fact that the order is so clear, it was entered before the trial even began, we're entitled to know who the witnesses are going to be for the upcoming two weeks and the order in which they're going to be called, and that's all we'd like. Also, it might be helpful if there was some indication as to what the relative importance of these witnesses was going to be because sometimes and apparently an insignificant witness turns out to be a very important one and apparently an important one turns out not to be so important after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you are saying, Mr. Sayers. That is, you're telling us something reasonable. It would be reasonable; it would be rational. It so happens that the Prosecutor is confronted with difficult circumstances and he explained on several occasions what that was about so we all know what's going on, and the difference between the reality and what is to be wished. But what I would like to say to Mr. Nice is that unless there is no testimony at all, unless there are a few days without witnesses, preparation should not be done in an improvised manner. I don't think we're trying to justify here the number of hearing days; that's not the problem. The problem is to reach the truth within a fair trial carried out under the best circumstances. I think I agree with what Mr. Sayers has just said, it needs -- some preparatory time is necessary both for the Defence and for the Trial Chamber, and that the Office of the Prosecutor must do its best, keeping in mind the difficulties that it is confronted with, and unless there is no hearing at all, but it would be better that the hearings be properly prepared and that the information arrive in advance. At least that's how I see things. I believe the problem is not to have a record number of witnesses but rather to have a system of evidence which is presented under the best conditions with the best preparation and the greatest fairness so that the Defence can present its case in the best way. I don't know whether Mr. Nice can improve things further, given the difficulties that he is faced with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As matter of history, I think the two-week order was pretty well immediately overtaken by our supplying 60 witnesses in the proposed order which was then supplanted by an even longer list, or longer list. We have always drawn to the Defence's attention every change in the order of witnesses as soon as we've known of it, so that it's always been my intention they should have much more than just a two-week running order. They should have the whole order of the witnesses as being forthcoming. If we stuck with the order itself, it would be restrictive on them and, I think, restrictive on everybody else. I always do my best to ensure that they have at least two weeks' notice of the witnesses, but I can just give you -- I think I started yesterday -- I'll give you an example of the things that have happened in the last two weeks. There was somebody who couldn't come because his child effectively ran away from school; that was one day's notice or two days' notice. There was somebody who couldn't come because a child was going to visit him, and a long-planned arrangement was suddenly jettisoned by him; he said, "I'm sorry, I'm not coming." Then somebody has been taken on military activity to a trouble spot that's arisen unexpectedly elsewhere in the world, and he's suddenly taken out of the list. These problems are happening all the time and mean that we have to reorganise the list. The witnesses further down the list, some of them are people who've got booked dates; that is to say, like the people who are coming next week, one of them in particular, he's booked his dates a long time in advance, and he can't really be moved from that slot. There's another witness, later on in the year, the rigidity of whose timetable is absolute, according to him and those who represent him. Therefore the problems of juggling witnesses is very, very considerable. All I can say is we do our very best. I think that both my friends and the Chamber will be heartened to discover what I'm going to tell you, in any event, about the listing of witnesses for the remainder of the trial. I can either do that now or later, but for the immediate forthcoming fortnight, the position is as follows. Carter comes in on Sunday, will be proofed on Sunday, and will start his evidence on Monday. Therefore the Defence are in a position to read Carter's statements, and I've instructed Ms. Somers to make available a summary, in draft form if necessary, on Sunday, as soon as it is available. Duncan, the brigadier or general, has given us just Tuesday and Wednesday. He comes in, I think, on Monday night and has to be out on Wednesday night. Happily, Carter is willing to be a sandwich if necessary; he can, I think, stay till Friday, so that if his evidence isn't finished on Monday, then he will be available on Friday. But although I may not be here for much of next week because I'm in Jelisic, I'm going to ask the Chamber and my friends, if they can, to deal with Carter on Monday; maybe the only way they can deal with that is by taking the summary as evidence in chief. And if Friday is free, Colonel Schipper, who was here yesterday and the day before but who had regimental appointments to deal with today -- and they'd been booked in advance, appointments to his regiment, people applying, so he really couldn't stand them up -- has agreed to be available on Friday. His summary or a preliminary summary will be served today. So that takes care of next week, and I hope one way or another the days will be full. For the following week, at the moment where we have only sittings on, I think, Thursday and Friday morning, it's Forgrave and Hay who are expected to be available. So that takes us the fortnight, I'm happy to say, and neither now or at a later stage I will tell you what I am going to do about the listing of all other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't keep us in suspense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber will recall that the question of outstanding witnesses was raised by me, and the Chamber responded to my offer of information by a Status Conference. But, nevertheless, I am carrying on doing exactly what I said I was going to do, which was to review all outstanding potential witnesses and to decide which ones, in our judgement, could provide evidence that the Chamber should have and which ones I could dispense with. The list of those witnesses will be with you not just on the week of the Status Conference, but next week and I hope at the beginning of next week. The list is going to be broken down into various categories which I have identified in the way I said I was going to; that is by looking first at the material that you should have and then deciding on the process by which we'll be able to make it available to you. So there will be a list of witnesses willing and to be called. They will be in the order I intend to call them. And that should, broadly speaking, cover the remaining witnesses for the trial. This isn't, obviously, an absolutely final position. It can't be. But it's where I am at the moment, in the common vernacular. The second category are witnesses who are at present unwilling, but in respect of whom I will be applying for subpoenas because I don't believe there is any reason why they should not respond to a subpoena. They are, I think, limited in number. One or two hands at most. The Chamber will recall that there might be witnesses who are unwilling, who I am not prepared to attempt at this moment to subpoena, because I judged that they may have good reasons for being unwilling, and in respect for whom I will in due course make an application to have their statements read. That category may be very small indeed. It may be effectively one or a couple of witnesses. And that's all. There will then be witnesses whose evidence can, in our submission, properly be taken by affidavit, and there are witnesses from other trials whose evidence can be given by testimony. They will be identified and can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: By transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, by transcript. And then there is then a small residual category of witnesses who we may apply to deal with one way or another, but about whom decisions are pending. Now, that material I hope will be available at the beginning of next week. It's being concluded at the moment. It will, I think, provide rather reassuring reading. I don't think we are going to be in the event above 100 witnesses to be called overall. And I remember one of the things Your Honour said at one stage. And it may even be ten less than that. I'm not sure at the moment. But that's the rough figures, I think. In addition to that material, the only other evidence that has to be dealt with is evidence in relation to the villages. And I've already explained how I am going to be dealing with that; namely, not by dossier. We better call them something else. By village binders. I will have provided for everyone extracts of material on a location-by-location basis the villages or occasions that have been worked on by individual investigators, and they, together, with one of the lawyers from my team will be able at convenient points in the remaining timetable of the trial to say, well, in respect to Busovaca, here are the documents that in light of the Tulica ruling we would invite the Chamber to accept. Our proposal is that these two witnesses or this witness or these three witnesses at most need be called. Alternatively, may now, in the judgement of the Chamber, be read, given all the other evidence that's in. So there will be a limited number of exercises, location by location, presenting documents and raising for discussion whether there are witnesses who need to be called. If there are witnesses to be called further on a location-by-location basis, they will be limited in number and they won't take very long. So that by next week I hope everyone will have a pretty final, not absolutely final, but pretty final list of witnesses to be called and in the order they are to be called. And once we've gone through the village binders or location binders, all the remaining witnesses will be identified as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may also give us a date when you anticipate the Prosecution closing. It would be helpful. You've got our timetable of hearings, although there is bound to be slippage one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't done a calculation yet, and therefore it's only a matter of feel at the moment. But I suspect we'll have something in the region of 20 witnesses for the new year, but I hope it won't be much more than that. In a way, that's a better guide than giving a time. I've already said, I think twice today, and once yesterday, the only way that we can accelerate the speed of witnesses, apart from -- no, there are two ways we can accelerate the speed of evidence. One is by taking summaries to some degree as evidence in chief. The other is by taking much more limited evidence from individual witnesses. I believe some of the outstanding witnesses, I can't have them all in my memory, I'm afraid, but some of the outstanding witnesses are witnesses who can be taken to very focused points of evidence and taken quite shortly. One or two of them, of course, are witnesses who may be long, because they are, for example, experts. But I hope that's reassuring, and it may not make the proposed Status Conference unnecessary, but it may make it in fact more useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's helpful. Anything the Defence want to say about that? It started as a response to your point, but went rather further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It was reassuring, obviously, Mr. President. But, as you point out, it was not in response to our point. Our concern is a little bit more tangible, if you like. We are the ones who have to prepare for the unexpected and so forth. And we would like two weeks' notice to the maximum extent possible. There may be, we realise, individual deviants from the two week requirement, but we don't think that it's unfair to insist upon what the Court has ordered. It makes it more expeditious to do the cross-examination. We can do it more professionally. It saves time. And it's what the Court's ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, of course you are right, that the original order was for two weeks' notice, and I think it's only reasonable to maintain it, but subject to individual circumstances that might call for a reconsideration. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour. And I completely agree, but I think, to use the exception rather than the rule should be that the -- we get the two weeks with exceptional -- exceptions in individual circumstances. Not that it should be exceptional for us to get the two weeks notice. And I'm not upbraiding the Prosecution. I really am not. I understand the constraints under which they work. But it really puts a very substantial burden upon the Defence not to have two weeks' notice of who the witnesses are going to be. It really does, for reasons that I don't think require explication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe we understand the situation, and we have to take a fair and realistic approach to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next point, I think, concerns the use of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It probably does, Judge, but in comparison to the other three points which I'd like to raise, it's relatively minor. Perhaps I can jump ahead. Although absent from the Court, I have been following the transcript with great care, and there are three things that continue to crop up that I think we might offer some assistance to the Court in terms of expeditious treatment. In quick order, they are a standing objection to any evidence outside the time frame of the indictment. Hearsay, a recurring issue. And last but not least, most important to us, the issue of what's been called facetiously tit-for-tat or the actions of the Muslims and the Serbs in this regard and why it's important. If I may cover them each briefly. I've done a little chart I'd like to hand up to the Court for its own edification. They can -- you can pitch it if you find it of no utility. It's essentially the amended indictment put in graphic form relative to the time frame set out in the counts. The time frame is different. But essentially the persecution count runs from November 1991 through March 31 of 1994. It is our position, as stated when the issues come up, that any evidence outside of the time frame be ruled inadmissible. We will continue to point that out to the Court, but I thought this chart might be somewhat useful. If not, or it's not graphically clear, it's my fault. We will continue, of course, to alert the Court when evidence as such comes in, but because the Prosecution has styled its indictment with regard to time frame differently, it's a little difficult to track. It's therefore incumbent on all of us to understand whether evidence is coming in pursuant to the all-encompassing persecution theory, in which case anything from November '91 to March of '94 is fair game. Or, alternatively, it's a more precise kind of evidence. The wilful killings, murder causing serious injury, counts 7 through 13 having a much more constrained time frame. We don't want to burden the record in the middle of the evidence of a witness with these continuing issues, so I thought I would bring this to the Court's attention at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that looks helpful. We will have in mind this document and we'll obviously look at the evidence accordingly. But, of course, if the Defence want to make an objection, they must be entitled to do so, particularly if it's an objection on grounds of lack of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, Judge. And what I had hoped was to persuade the Court that we have what's called a standing objection. That's an United States term. For evidence outside the time frame of the indictment. So that we need not burden the Court each and every time. On the other hand, I like to think that our objections assist the Court in alerting the Court to the issues as we see them. So I am not trying to obviate our responsibility and just we are going to sit like potted palms. On the other hand, I would like to alert the Court to this issue and have a standing objection to any purported evidence outside the time frame of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't like the concept of a standing objection. I think the objection should be taken individually in relation to a particular point because the fact that there is evidence outside the time frame doesn't necessarily mean that it's irrelevant, but that I can see that a question of relevance will arise. There could also be a question of prejudice. But I think that it would be more useful to take it as it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And I understood that and anticipate that different judges react differently to the suggestion. I thought I'd at least hand it up to the Court. We enjoy having our objections overruled. We enjoy being the losers from time to time, but we enjoy making them when we have to make them. Moving along up the ladder is the issue of hearsay. I understand, because I have seen the record, the issue, the Tadic issue, that hearsay is not of itself inadmissible. I would just like to say this once so we won't have to say it at all. The use of hearsay, third, fourth hand, not only is unreliable, but it makes it impossible for us to recreate the event and challenge the event that's being discussed. It's impossible, often, because the identity of the ultimate declarant is hidden. The Court, of course, is not insensitive to that. Last, but not least, it has the reality effect of shifting both the burden of proof and the burden of presumption to us, because once hearsay is on the record, then it becomes for us at the close of the evidence to point out under the rules exactly where we think the hearsay that has been admitted should be deemed unreliable and not put in your judgement. And it makes our investigation into the facts more difficult when we are tracing down hearsay that is third, fourth hand. The issue, of course, needs to be resolved each and every time it comes up, but having said what I have to say, I hope the Court will have in its mind these difficult issues for the Defence when hearsay, which the Court usually spots before we make an objection, or in conjunction with our objection, has to rule on this difficult issue. I understand that as a general matter hearsay is not inadmissible and the Court specifically makes rulings as to when it is. We are just trying to persuade the Court again, and in this fashion, when we have a little time, as opposed to making a speech each time, to think about the difficulty and the practical reality shifting of production and proof that the admissibility of hearsay results in. Last, but not least, and most important to us, there have been several exchanges between Your Honour and counsel with regard to cross-examination that is trying to illicit crimes committed by Muslims against Croats, or Serbs for that matter, against Croats. And Your Honour has opined on a variety of times the relevance. I'd like to reply to that now because it's an important part of our case. Crimes committed against Croats, the whole side of the triangle, if you will, goes mens rea, goes to motivation for acts, actions, defensive or offensive position, and ultimately, and I hope we never get here, goes to mitigation. In summary fashion, what I am trying to say is there is an entire milieu in which the actions in the Lasva Valley occurred. The office of the Prosecution would have you look at one part of the triangle, the Croat part, saying there are offences committed on all sides. Just look at the Croats. That's all we are here to worry about. If you do that, you will never see the entire triangle. What I am trying to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stein, as regards this question, very quickly. I think that the objection that was raised is not to the murder committed or other criminal acts that were committed against the Croats as such, but rather the fact that they have been covered as such and not in relation to the indictment. Because from a legal point of view, the fact that there were murders of Croats does not justify murders committed by Croats of Muslims or Serbs. Therefore, that was the point. Now, you are telling us that that relates to mens rea, the defensive or offensive positions, of course, but we have to start from that point and move toward the murders or other criminal acts that were committed against Croats and not to deal with the criminal acts committed against the Croats as such, in and of themselves. We have to stay with the indictment. If you make the relationship between the criminal acts and the indictment, of course that's clear and possible, because there is the questions of legitimate defence and motivation, mens rea, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Perhaps it's my fault, and I am trying to be clear. We are not justifying actions. We did this because they did that. That is not my point. What I am saying is the context in which the acts occurred, while not justification for the act, and again our position generally on these things is that Mr. Kordic had nothing to do with it, but that the acts occurred in a milieu. And you can only understand what happened in the valley if you understand the milieu. The question, of course, is how far into that we get. Mr. Nice, in fact, opened this issue in his opening at page 74, where he raised for the record the question of whether the Croat complaints about the behaviour of the Bosniaks and the Mujahedins were "genuine and well founded or was a smoke screen." So the Prosecutor's themselves have kicked off, if you will, the issue, if nothing else, to set it up to put it down. The statutes, of course, of the Tribunal require you to look at the wilful actions of the accused, whether the circumstances under which he acted were unjustifiable. There is an issue of military necessity. But most important, and I don't think this is apparent initially until I read it yesterday, the exculpatory nature of the evidence that we are trying to get in goes to not only exculpation but as to sentencing under Rule 101(B), (ii) and (iii). 101(B), (ii) and (iii) incorporate by reference the concept of mitigating circumstances as well as the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia. Under Article 56, paragraph 2 of the Croatian Criminal Code, and I'll quote briefly: "All the circumstances which result in a less or more serious punishment for the perpetrator of a criminal offence, the motives for committing the criminal offence, the circumstances under which the criminal offence was committed, the conditions in which the perpetrator had lived prior to committing the offence, as well as the totality of social and personal grounds which contributed to the perpetration of the offence --" shall be considered. And I want to be clear. I've quoted from that skipping along. I mean, I haven't quoted the whole paragraph. That's again Article 56, part 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In my view, Mr. Stein, the issue's a very difficult legal one jurisprudentially. It's not fully settled. The statute of the International Criminal Court does provide for self-defence to be raised as a defence, but in determining the extent to which is legitimate as a defence, the whole question of proportionality is exceedingly important. So for my own purposes I've always considered it relevant, particularly when it is raised in a context of defence, as a defensive strategy, but I think ultimately the question of proportionality will be very, very significant. But I think it's an important legal issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. And that, of course, goes to how you view these things. And I can't do them in an abstract. I was not the scholar I would like to have been at law school. The abstract is difficult, the specifics in which they are raised are better. But I wanted to take advantage of the time that we have today without a witness present to at least put this on the record fully and completely. The other thing that's important from our perspective and you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree. We agree that we are not conducting a trial of certain Muslims or Muslims milieu that are not included in the indictment. Insofar as you agree with that, that's fine. You must not pull us into things which could be considered outside the subject. If you are within the scope of the subject, then it's fine. I think that is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I am trying to do that and I hope that is what everyone understands I am trying to say. The only final thing I would like to say on that is some of the witnesses who come before you present our only chance to ask about these issues. Theoretically, we can recall them and extend the trial, but much of what our case is will be made through the cross-examination of the witnesses. There will be no other opportunity. I don't want to have to go through the difficulties that my colleague has gone through in retrieving these witnesses. So that I ask when Your Honour rules on the issues that come up that you consider these difficult problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The final point, I suppose, can be dealt with in this way. You can, of course, deal with it in cross-examination. That does have the virtue of your not having to call any evidence about it. But I anticipate that, at least for some of these matters, you are going to call evidence, in which case then it becomes rather less necessary to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Frankly, putting together the defence case as I have been, that's one of the issues I wanted to raise. I now sense the Court's attitude is not to preclude me from doing all of this, as long as it's within the parameters of the indictment with reference to a specific defence recognised or at least suggested by the statutes and of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I am not encouraging you to call up large numbers of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I will call -- Judge, I will take that as a touchstone for our presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me -- well, we'll have to deal with all of that in due course. Let me go back to the matters that you indicated made this sort of evidence admissible or made it relevant, and see that I've got it right. You said it was relevant to mens rea, motivation, and there was a third point, which I think was litigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It was meant to be mitigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mitigation. That makes it very different. And that, of course, is the sentencing point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take the final point quite clearly. As far as the first two are concerned, mens rea, what's the relevance of it, this sort of evidence to mens rea?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right. The statutes under which we are operating each have a defined mens rea or an implied mens rea, but they each have a mental aspect to them. There is wilful conduct, unjustifiable conduct, and other terms. The context in which the conduct occurred is either wholly just one day the Croats decided to do this, in which case the Prosecution has its best situation, or it's in reaction to, perhaps an overreaction, but nonetheless a reaction to some other event. It's never been my practice to lecture or to suggest to the Court how to read the law. We will certainly set out the law in our closing papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. Now, what I am asking you to do is to apply your submissions to the law. Then -- you haven't mentioned self-defence. Is that part of your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In the context of what I am saying, the answer is yes. Now, I want to be clear, we are -- and we have to be fact specific and village specific. Sometimes the answer is no. Sometimes the answer is yes. So it depends very specifically about where and when. And certainly the concept of self-defence evolves over time as you march through, from the times that the Muslims and Croats were cooperating to the time that the coalitions broke down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't forget, Mr. Stein, that when you speak about legitimate defence, this is covered by individual responsibility. We are not dealing with legitimate defence of a collective community or country or region. We are speaking about individual criminal responsibility, and it's within that framework that legitimate defence can be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And we have individual as well as command responsibility issues, and the mens rea for each appears and will be argued to be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And motivation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's right, sir. Again, motivation. If one morning a group of Croats decided to just start up and do something, that's a clearly different issue than if a village is part of a military campaign, it is in an essentially strategic area, indeed the attack may have gone awry or there may have been more consequential damages, collateral damages than anticipated. Those are the kinds of issues. Now, again, every time I stand up and talk about this, I want to give the big caveat that our client was not in charge of the military. But to some extent, in order to understand the events that went on, since the Prosecution is claiming he was part of the military establishment, we have unfortunately been forced to have this burden on our shoulders to give you a clear explication of what went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may at some stage be helpful if you indicate -- and of course we have in mind that these are foundation issues, or background issues, were-the-crimes-committed issues, not issues as to whether your client or his co-accused was involved in the crimes. But even with that in mind, it may be helpful at some stage if we have a document from you in response, perhaps, to the dossiers when they come, as to what it is the Defence say in each case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Glad to help out, and as long as we have them in a reasonable period of time that we can produce a response, and reasoned response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So there is no question of doing that in any hurry, but when you are able to do it. Yes. Now, we shall have to have a break in a moment. Were there any other issues you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We have two other issues on my plate. I'll defer to Mr. Sayers in a moment. The site visit as well as the issues regarding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this may be a matter which is better deal with in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Agreed. The only other public issue, that we can deal with whenever Your Honour directs us, is exhibits and notes and diaries; again, a recurring problem that comes up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Deal with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good. We have been put on notice --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We can tell, when we read the discovery material from the witness statement, that a witness has a diary or attachments to the statement itself to the Prosecutor. Immediately upon reading such, we send a letter to the Prosecutor: "Can we see the diary or the attachments or the contemporaneous notes?" We, I don't believe, save one instance, have ever seen them before the witness testifies. The witness comes on board with notes, a diary, and these kinds of matters, referred to or not, to refresh or not. But by the time we get done analysing the legal issues as to whether or not we're entitled to see them, we get them in the middle of the examination, problem one; sometimes they're not in a language we speak, problem two. We are therefore requesting the Court that -- and suggest to the Prosecution -- that when such diaries, notes, and things are patently apparent from the witness statements and we ask our colleagues for them, that we have them so we don't have to elongate the trial fighting about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before you rule, I want to be clear. As to personal letters or correspondence, we're not interested. As to documents that have clearly been written to record events, and/or handed to the Prosecution, or documents or notes or attachments that are actually part of the statement given to the Prosecution, we believe that these are important. And certainly if the Prosecution has an objection, they can tell us by way of a written response. But we're not getting these things in time to effectively use them and analyse them for your inspection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've already dealt with this, that clearly, if the Prosecutor has material which should be disclosed from a witness, then they're under a duty to disclose it. If, on the other hand, as does seem to happen, the witness has a diary, which he either brings with him or not -- if he doesn't bring it with him, there's nothing anybody can do with it. If, on the other hand, he does bring the diary and refers to it in his examination, then it's in issue as to whether you should be able to look at it or not. It would partly depend on whether there is any private matter; in most cases not. I suspect that the difficulty is that the Prosecution don't have sight of this or knowledge of it until the witness comes. Mr. Nice, is that broadly the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is indeed broadly the position. Wherever material is available and is effectively part of the statement, we serve it. Wherever there is a request made by the Defence for a diary or similar document that is apparently identified in the statement, we convey the request to the witness, as soon as we get the request from the Defence, and respond in accordance with what the witness tells us. Wherever a witness turns up with his diary, we ask if he wishes to refer to it and if he wishes to make it available to us. I think that's the appropriate regime for us to continue. But I have no desire to keep material back and every desire to make material available because it accelerates the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, is there anything else in open session that anybody wants to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I think the rest should be in closed session, if Your Honour so chooses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Provided it's not a lengthy matter, we'll deal with it before the break. Very well. Go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 11.05 a.m., to be followed by an ex parte
